summary: This unit teaches you to terminate and connect cables that need special methods: armoured power cable, mineral-insulated and fire-resistant cable, coaxial cable, twisted-pair data cable, screened control cable and, for awareness, optical fibre. You will learn to plan the work, strip each cable without damage, fit the right glands, lugs, ferrules and connectors, test the finished terminations and record the results.

blocks.p: Ordinary sheathed cable is stripped and connected with a few hand tools. **Specialist cables** are built differently, for strength, fire survival or carrying signals, and each has its own way of being stripped, sealed, glanded and connected. Get it wrong and an armoured cable loses its earth path, a mineral-insulated cable soaks up moisture, a TV picture breaks up, or a network link fails its test.
This unit is for Level 2 trainees, who terminate cables under supervision with the circuits isolated and proved dead. Tests on finished cables are made or checked by a competent person.

head: Cable
What makes it special
Where it is used in Jamaica
rows: Steel wire armoured (SWA) and other armoured cable
A layer of steel wires protects the cores
Buried supplies to pump houses, gate motors, outbuildings and street lights; factories, hotels and farms
Copper conductors in magnesium oxide powder inside a copper sheath; survives fire
Fire alarm and emergency lighting circuits, boiler rooms and hot places
Special insulation keeps working for a time in a fire
Fire alarm and emergency lighting circuits
A centre conductor inside a screen, for radio-frequency signals
TV and satellite outlets, CCTV cameras, radio antennas
Four twisted pairs carry network data
Computer networks in offices, schools, hotels and homes; IP cameras and Wi-Fi points
A foil or braid screen keeps out electrical interference
Factories, water treatment and pumping stations, building controls
Internet and phone networks, links between buildings

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Isolate and prove dead before terminating; control cuts, sharp armour ends, glass slivers, invisible laser light and test voltages.
Read the wiring diagram and termination schedule; choose glands, lugs, ferrules, markers and tools; check bending radius and space.
Fit the gland parts, strip the sheath, cut the armour without damaging the bedding, clamp the armour and connect the earth tag.
Strip, test, fit the pot and seal quickly, and test again for moisture.
Fit F, BNC and RJ45 connectors and punch down data outlets, keeping screens and twists correct.
Terminate screened and multicore control cable
Mark every core, fit ferrules, terminate to the schedule and earth the screen at one end.
Choose and crimp lugs and ferrules with the right tool and tighten terminals to the maker's torque.
Carry out continuity, insulation resistance and wire-map tests and write the results on the job sheet.

blocks.p: Read the safety and planning section first, then the general terminating skills, then the section for each type of cable. Strip lengths, torques and test values come from the cable, gland or connector maker: the figures in this kit are typical, so always follow the maker's instructions and your instructor.

Before you terminate a cable into a panel, distribution board or isolator, the equipment is **isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead**. Switch off the isolator or main switch, fit your own lock and keep the key, fix a danger tag with your name, the date and the reason, then prove your tester on a proving unit, test between every pair of conductors at the point of work, and **prove the tester again**. The second check shows the tester did not fail during the test. Remember that the incoming terminals of a board can stay live when its main switch is off.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Cut away from your body and away from the hand holding the cable; never hold the cable on your leg; keep blades sharp and covered
Sharp ends: wear gloves and safety glasses; bend the cut ends away from you
Glass fibre slivers and invisible laser light
See the optical fibre section: never look into a fibre end
Point it away from people and cables you are not working on; the nozzle stays hot
Keep fingers out of the dies; use as the maker says
The tester produces 500 V or more: warn others, do not touch the cable during the test, and let the tester discharge it afterwards
Isopropyl alcohol is flammable: small amounts, closed bottle, good airflow

ul: Read the **wiring diagram** and the **termination schedule**: they say which core goes to which terminal at each end, and the core numbers or colours.
Check the cable type, size and number of cores against the drawing.
Choose the **gland** that matches the cable's outside diameter and armour, and the entry thread of the enclosure.

Check there is room in the enclosure, and that the cable can enter without bending tighter than the maker allows. As a guide, many armoured and MI cables should not be bent tighter than about **6 times their overall diameter**, and twisted-pair data cable not tighter than about **4 times**.
List the materials: glands and earth tags, lugs or ferrules, core markers, sleeving, heat-shrink, cable ties and labels.
List the tools: cable knife and sheath stripper, hacksaw, wire strippers, crimp tools and dies, torque screwdriver, and the test instruments.
Agree the time with your supervisor and the customer, especially if a supply must be switched off.
Plan the tests and have a sheet ready to record the results.

Use a sheath stripper or cable knife, always **cutting away from your body**. Make a shallow ring cut, then a lengthwise cut, and peel the sheath off. Do not cut so deep that you score the insulation, bedding or pairs underneath.
Measure strip lengths from the gland, connector or terminal maker's chart, and mark them before cutting.
Strip each core to the length the terminal needs: the insulation goes right up to the terminal, with **no bare conductor showing** outside it and no strands left out.

blocks.p: Fine-stranded flexible conductors are fitted with a crimped **bootlace ferrule** before they go into a screw terminal. The ferrule holds all the strands together so none splay out or are cut by the screw. Choose the ferrule for the conductor size; insulated ferrules are colour-coded by size, but the colours differ between makers' systems, so read the size on the packet. Crimp with a ferrule crimper, which squeezes it into a square or other shape that fits the terminal.

blocks.note: Do not tin a stranded conductor with solder before putting it into a screw terminal. Under the pressure of the screw the solder slowly creeps, the screw loosens, and the joint can overheat. Use a ferrule.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Choose the lug to match the **conductor size** (for example 16 mm² or 6 AWG), the **stud or bolt size** it goes on, and the conductor material: copper lugs for copper, and bimetal lugs where aluminium conductors connect to copper bars.
Strip the insulation to the depth of the lug barrel without cutting any strands, and push the conductor fully in so all the strands are inside.

Crimp with the tool and **die** made for that lug size, in the place and number of crimps the maker shows. A **ratchet crimper** will not open until the full crimp has been made, so every crimp is complete. Large lugs are crimped with a **hydraulic crimper**, worked by oil pressure.
Check the crimp by eye, then give it a **firm pull test**.
Cover the barrel with heat-shrink or a sleeve, in the right colour where the job needs it, and bolt the lug to the stud at the right torque.

blocks.p: Small pre-insulated crimp terminals are commonly colour-coded: **red** for about 0.5 to 1.5 mm², **blue** for about 1.5 to 2.5 mm², **yellow** for about 4 to 6 mm². Use the matching coloured die position on the crimp tool.

Terminal screws and lug bolts are tightened to the maker's **torque** value, printed on the device or in its instructions in newton metres (N·m). Use a **torque screwdriver** or torque wrench set to that value. Too loose, and the joint has a high resistance and overheats; too tight, and the conductor is crushed or the terminal cracked.

ul: Fit a **core marker** on each core of a multicore cable, with the number from the termination schedule, so every core can be traced to its terminal.
Mark the cores before cutting them to length, so none get mixed up.
Dress the cores neatly, with gentle bends and no strain on the terminals, and tie them with cable ties not pulled so tight that they crush the insulation.
Where a flexible cord enters a plug or an appliance, the **cord grip** (cord anchorage) must clamp the outer sheath, so a pull on the cord does not reach the conductors.

blocks.h: How an armoured cable is built

head: Layer, from the centre out
What it does
rows: Copper (or aluminium) cores that carry the current
PVC or XLPE round each core; coloured or numbered to identify it
A plastic layer that cushions the cores under the armour
Galvanised steel wires that protect the cable from damage and can act as an earth path
PVC or low-smoke sheath that keeps out water and protects the armour from corrosion

blocks.p: **SWA** stands for **steel wire armoured**. Single-core cables carrying AC use aluminium wire armour instead, because steel round a single core would heat up from induced currents. Cables made to US standards with a metal sheath (such as metal-clad, MC, cable) use their own connectors, but the ideas are the same.

blocks.h: Parts of an armoured cable gland

head: Part
What it does
rows: A plastic cover over the gland that keeps out water and dirt and protects the gland from corrosion
Seal round the outer sheath, keeping water out (outdoor-type glands)
Grip the armour wires between them and connect them to the gland body
Screws into the enclosure or passes through the hole, held by a locknut
Fitted on the entry thread to connect the gland, and so the armour, to the earth bar with a conductor
Hold the gland in the enclosure; the washer keeps the enclosure's IP rating

blocks.p: Indoor-type glands grip the armour but have no outer seal. Outdoor-type glands add a seal on the outer sheath, and some types also seal the inner bedding. Use the type the drawing gives for the place: an indoor gland outdoors lets water run down the armour into the enclosure.

blocks.h: Terminating an armoured cable into a gland

flow: Isolate and prove dead; choose the gland to match the cable size
Slide the shroud, then the back nut and seal, onto the cable
Mark the sheath and armour cut positions from the gland maker's chart
Remove the outer sheath with a cable knife, cutting away from you
Cut the armour: saw part way through each wire with a hacksaw at the mark, then bend the wire to break it off
Check the bedding and inner insulation are not damaged
Fit the gland body and earth tag to the enclosure with the locknut
Spread the armour evenly over the cone, push on the clamping ring and tighten the body so the armour is gripped
Tighten the back nut to seal on the outer sheath; slide the shroud over the gland
Connect the earth tag to the earth bar; terminate the cores

blocks.note: When cutting the armour, never cut right through the wires into the bedding. A hacksaw that goes too deep cuts the bedding and the insulation of the cores, and the damage may only show up on the insulation test, or years later as a fault.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The armour must make a good connection to earth through the gland and earth tag, so that a fault on any core trips the protective device. Many specifications also use a spare core or a separate conductor as the circuit's protective conductor. Follow the drawing.

**MICC** stands for **mineral-insulated copper-clad** (or copper-covered) cable. Solid copper conductors run inside a seamless copper sheath, packed in **magnesium oxide powder**. Often a plastic outer cover, commonly red for fire alarm circuits, is added for corrosion protection and identification.

head: Property
Why it matters
rows: Copper and magnesium oxide do not burn, so the circuit keeps working while fire alarm sounders and emergency lights are needed
Suits boiler rooms, kitchens and hot plant
The copper sheath is strong and can serve as the protective conductor
No separate earth conductor is usually needed
**The powder takes in moisture from the air (it is hygroscopic)**
A stripped end left open soaks up moisture and its insulation resistance falls; the end must be sealed soon after stripping

flow: Plan the length; slide the gland parts onto the cable
Strip the copper sheath back with a rotary or ratchet stripper, without nicking the conductors
Clean all loose powder from the conductors and the end
Test insulation resistance between conductors and from each conductor to the sheath
Screw the brass **pot** squarely onto the sheath
Fill the pot with sealing compound from one side, so no air is trapped
Fit the seal cap or disc, crimp it, and fit insulating sleeves on the conductors
Test the insulation resistance again
Fit the gland and connect to the equipment

ul: Seal the end as soon as you can after stripping. In Jamaica's humid air an open end can take in moisture within minutes to hours.
After sealing, the insulation resistance reading should be **high and steady**. A reading that **falls slowly** during the test means moisture is still in the cable or the seal.

The usual cure is to cut the end back past the damp part, strip and seal again, and test again. Some electricians drive moisture out with gentle heat; do this only if you have been trained and your instructor allows it.
Many electricians test again after about 24 hours: a sound seal holds its reading.

blocks.p: Fire alarm and emergency lighting circuits must keep working during a fire, so they are run in MI cable or **fire-resistant cable**, which keeps working for a set time in a fire. The cable is only as good as its support: plastic clips and cable ties melt in a fire and let cables fall, where they can be damaged or trap firefighters. Fix these cables with **metal clips or fire-rated fixings**, as the specification says, and keep them separate from other circuits.

head: Part, from the centre out
What it does
rows: Insulating foam or solid plastic that keeps the centre exactly in the middle
Carries the return signal and keeps interference out
The outer sheath that protects the cable

blocks.p: The size and spacing of these parts give the cable its **impedance**. TV, satellite and CCTV video use **75 ohm** coax, such as RG6 for TV and satellite and RG59 for older CCTV. Radio and some antenna systems use **50 ohm** coax. Use the type the equipment needs.

head: Connector
Use
rows: TV and satellite outlets and equipment. The **compression** type is the most reliable; it is squeezed on with a compression tool.
CCTV cameras and recorders, and test equipment; locks with a quarter-turn bayonet.
Larger 50 ohm radio and antenna connections.
TV aerial sockets on equipment made to British and European standards.

flow: Check the connector suits the coax type and size
Cut the end square with sharp cutters, without crushing the cable
Strip the jacket, braid and dielectric to the maker's lengths with a coax stripping tool set for the cable
Fold the braid back over the jacket neatly and trim stray strands
Check that **no braid strand touches the centre conductor**
Push the connector on until the dielectric is level with the inside of the connector
Check the centre conductor sticks out only the short length the maker gives, often about 2 mm
Squeeze it fully in the compression tool
Pull-test, then test continuity and check there is no short from centre to screen

ul: A single braid strand touching the centre conductor **shorts the signal**: the TV or camera gets no picture.

Do not crush or kink coax, and do not drive staples into it: crushing changes the spacing inside, and so the impedance, and causes signal loss and reflections. Use clips made for coax and keep bends gentle.
Outdoors, use weatherproof connectors or boots, and leave a **drip loop** so water runs off before it reaches the connector.

Where an outdoor coax, such as from a satellite dish or roof antenna, enters a building, the code usually requires its screen to be **earthed (grounded)** through an earthing block, to protect against lightning surges.

blocks.p: With a multimeter on continuity or resistance: the centre conductor should show continuity end to end, the screen should show continuity end to end, and there must be **no continuity between the centre and the screen**. A signal meter checks the TV signal level at the outlet.

A data cable such as **Cat 6** has **four twisted pairs** (eight conductors) in one sheath: blue, orange, green and brown, each twisted with a white or white-striped partner. **UTP** stands for **unshielded twisted pair**; screened types (such as F/UTP) add a foil screen.

Each pair is twisted so that interference picked up along the cable affects both wires equally and cancels out, and so that signals in one pair do not leak into the next (**crosstalk**). Each pair has a different twist rate, and the twists must be kept as close as possible to the termination.

head: Category
Typical performance
rows: Up to 1 Gb/s over 100 m, and 10 Gb/s over shorter runs (about 55 m)

blocks.p: A twisted-pair Ethernet **channel**, from device to device, may be up to **100 m**: usually up to **90 m** of fixed cable (the permanent link, from patch panel to wall outlet) plus up to 10 m of patch leads in total.

Use **one standard** for the whole installation, at both ends of every cable and lead, as the specification says. A lead wired T568B at one end and T568A at the other swaps the orange and green pairs (a crossover). Modern equipment rarely needs a crossover lead, so it shows up on the tester as a wiring fault.

blocks.h: Making a patch lead with RJ45 plugs

flow: Cut the cable to length and slide the plug boots on first
Strip about 25 to 40 mm of sheath without nicking the pairs
Untwist each pair only as far as needed and lay the wires flat in the standard's order
Trim the ends straight, about 12 mm from the sheath, so they reach the front of the plug
Push them into the plug, clip side down, with the sheath going inside the plug under its clamp
Check through the plug that the order is right and each wire reaches the end
Crimp with the data crimp tool; repeat at the other end
Test with a cable tester

blocks.p: The **RJ45** plug is properly called an **8P8C** (eight positions, eight contacts) modular plug.

ul: Data outlets (jacks) and patch panels use insulation-displacement contacts (IDCs). The wires are pressed into the slots with a **punch-down tool**, which seats each wire and cuts off the spare end; the blade faces the waste side.
Follow the colour label on the jack for the standard in use (A or B).
Keep the sheath as close to the jack as possible and **untwist as little as possible**: no more than about **13 mm** of any pair. Untwisting more raises crosstalk and can fail the test.
Do not strip the insulation: the IDC cuts through it to make contact.
Keep data cable apart from power cables; never in the same conduit or trunking compartment. Cross power at right angles.
Do not pull harder than the maker allows (often about 110 N for a four-pair cable), kink it, crush it under staples or over-tighten cable ties. Hook-and-loop straps are kinder than plastic ties.
Keep bends to at least about 4 times the cable diameter.
Label both ends of every cable with the outlet number.

blocks.p: A **wire-map tester** checks that each of the eight wires goes from the right pin to the right pin, and shows **opens** (a broken wire), **shorts**, **reversed pairs** (the two wires of a pair swapped), **crossed pairs** (pairs on the wrong pins) and, on better testers, **split pairs** (wires from two different pairs used as one pair). A split pair passes a simple continuity check but fails in use. Certification testers also measure length, loss and crosstalk against the category's limits.

Instrument signals, such as a 4 to 20 mA signal from a level sensor or a data link between controllers, are small and easily upset by **electrical interference** from motors, variable-speed drives and power cables. A **screen** of foil or braid around the cores catches the interference and carries it to earth. A foil screen has a bare **drain wire** running along it, used to connect the screen.

ul: Unless the drawing says otherwise, the screen is **earthed at one end only**, usually at the control-panel end. Earthing both ends can let current flow round the screen between two earth points that are at slightly different voltages (an **earth loop**), which itself causes interference.
At the other end, cut the screen and drain wire back and insulate them with sleeving or heat-shrink, so they cannot touch the enclosure or a terminal.
Where a cable passes through a junction box, keep the screen continuous: join the drain wires on an insulated terminal.
Keep instrument cables apart from power cables, and cross them at right angles.
Work from the termination schedule: core numbers, terminal numbers and both ends.
Mark every core before cutting, fit ferrules on stranded cores, terminate to the schedule and tighten to torque.
Dress the cores neatly into trunking or along the terminal rail, with spare cores marked, insulated and left long enough to use later.

blocks.p: An optical fibre carries light along a glass **core** surrounded by glass **cladding**, inside protective buffer, strength yarns and a jacket. Fibres are terminated by splicing on pre-made ends (pigtails) with a fusion splicer, by mechanical splices, or by using pre-terminated cables, usually by specialists. Common connectors are SC, LC and ST. Single-mode fibre cables are often yellow; multimode often orange or aqua.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: **Invisible light**: fibre systems use infrared light (for example 850, 1310 and 1550 nm) that you cannot see, which can damage your eyes

**Never look into a fibre end or connector**, even if you think it is dark. Make sure the equipment at the far end is off, keep dust caps on, and use an optical power meter, not your eyes, to check for light
**Glass slivers**: cleaved fibre ends are tiny, very sharp and almost invisible; they go into skin and eyes
Wear safety glasses; work on a dark mat so you can see them; pick them up with tape or tweezers and put them in a **marked, sealed container**; never brush them onto the floor or blow them away
No eating or drinking at the fibre bench; wash your hands after work
Isopropyl alcohol is flammable: small amounts, closed bottle

sections.title: Glands, IP ratings, testing and finishing

ul: The gland must match the **cable's outside diameter** (each gland size covers a range) and, for armoured cable, the armour size. Too big, and it neither grips nor seals; too small, and it will not fit or it crushes the cable.
It must match the **entry thread** of the enclosure, such as M20 or M25 metric, or ½ inch or ¾ inch NPT.
It must suit the place: indoor or outdoor type, and the IP rating needed.
A correctly sized and tightened gland **grips** the cable, so a pull cannot reach the terminals, and **seals** it, keeping out water and dust.

blocks.p: An **IP (ingress protection)** rating such as **IP65** has two figures. The first (0 to 6) says how well solids and dust are kept out; the second (0 to 8, and 9 on some equipment) says how well water is kept out. The higher the figure, the better the protection. A gland and its sealing washer must keep the enclosure's rating.

head: Figure
First figure: solids
Second figure: water
rows: Objects over 1 mm, such as wires
Continuous immersion, as the maker states

blocks.p: Equipment made for the US market may show a **NEMA type** instead, such as 3R (rain-resistant outdoors) or 4X (watertight and corrosion-resistant).
Before tests, the cable is isolated, proved dead and **disconnected from equipment at both ends**.

head: Test
How
Good result
rows: With a low-resistance ohmmeter, link a core to the earth (or another core) at the far end and measure at the near end; do the same for the armour or protective conductor
A low reading: the core is unbroken and connected at both ends
Check each core arrives at the right terminal at both ends
With an insulation tester, usually at **500 V DC** for 110/220 V circuits, between every pair of cores and from each core to earth (armour)
A high reading in **megohms (MΩ)**; new cable usually reads hundreds of megohms or more. Many standards set 1 MΩ as the least acceptable for circuits of this voltage.

ul: A **low** insulation reading means damaged insulation, moisture or a core touching the armour: find and fix it before the cable is used.
Warn people before an insulation test, do not touch the cable during it, and let the tester discharge the cable after.
Never insulation-test data, coax or control cables with electronic equipment still connected: 500 V can destroy it.
Data: wire-map test of every link and patch lead; certification tests where the specification asks for them.
Coax: continuity of centre and screen, no short between them; signal level at the outlet.
Fibre: done by specialists with a light source and power meter, never by eye.
Insulation right up to each terminal; no bare conductor or stray strands; ferrules and lugs the right size and firmly crimped.
Each core pull-checked and tightened to torque; core markers matching the drawing.
Glands the right size, tight and sealed; earth tags connected; shrouds fitted.
Cables neatly dressed and tied, with no tight bends.
Covers refitted; off-cuts, sheath strips and armour wire cleaned out of the enclosure.
Waste sorted: copper and steel for scrap, plastic waste in the bin, fibre slivers in the sealed container.
The job sheet completed with the cable labels, test results and any problems, for your supervisor.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can isolate and prove dead before terminating, and explain why the tester is proved again afterwards.
I can name the specialist cables in this unit and say where each is used.
I can plan a termination from a wiring diagram and termination schedule, including gland size and bending radius.
I can strip a sheath safely with a cable knife, cutting away from my body.
I can choose and crimp ferrules and lugs, pull-test them and tighten terminals to torque.
I can name the layers of an armoured cable and the parts of its gland.
I can terminate an armoured cable into a gland without damaging the bedding, and connect its earth tag.
I can explain why MI cable must be sealed quickly, seal it, and read a falling insulation reading.
I can explain why fire alarm cables need metal or fire-rated fixings.
I can name the parts of coax and fit a compression F connector with no braid touching the centre.
I can wire an RJ45 plug to T568B, punch down a data outlet with very little untwisting, and test it with a wire-map tester.
I can state the 100 m channel limit for twisted-pair Ethernet.
I can explain why an instrument cable's screen is earthed at one end only, and insulate the other end.
I can explain the dangers of optical fibre and handle off-cuts safely.
I can read an IP rating and choose a gland that grips and seals.
I can carry out continuity and insulation resistance tests and explain the readings.
I can finish the job, sort the waste and complete the job sheet.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Impedance of TV, satellite and CCTV coax / radio coax
In a Cat 5e or Cat 6 data cable
Twisted-pair Ethernet channel: fixed cable plus patch leads
Most untwisting allowed at a data termination
Typical least bending radius for armoured and MI cable; check the maker
Least bending radius for twisted-pair data cable
Usual insulation test voltage and a common minimum for 110/220 V cables
Dust-tight and protected against water jets

terms: Steel wires under the outer sheath that protect a cable and can act as an earth path.
The plastic layer between the cores and the armour.
A coax connector with a quarter-turn bayonet lock, used for CCTV.
A metal tube crimped on a fine-stranded conductor before it goes into a screw terminal.
A signal in one pair leaking into another pair.
The insulation between the centre conductor and the screen of a coax cable.
The bare wire along a foil screen, used to connect the screen to earth.
An unwanted current path when a screen is earthed at two points at different voltages.
A washer with a tab that connects a gland to the earth bar.
The screw-on coax connector used for TV and satellite.
A fitting that grips and seals a cable where it enters an enclosure.
Ingress protection: how well an enclosure keeps out solids and water.
Mineral-insulated copper-clad cable, insulated with magnesium oxide powder.
The brass fitting screwed onto the end of an MI cable and filled with sealing compound.
A tool that presses data wires into the slots of an outlet or patch panel and trims them.
The eight-pin modular plug used on data patch leads.
Foil or braid around cores that keeps out electrical interference.
A list of which core goes to which terminal at each end of a cable.
A screwdriver that tightens to a set turning force.
A test that shows whether each wire of a data cable goes to the right pin.

c1.title: Armoured cable to a pump house near Christiana
c1.text: Electrician Mr Errol Watson and trainee Brittany Hinds are terminating a 3-core steel wire armoured (SWA) cable from a farm's main panel to a pump-house isolator near Christiana, Manchester. The cable's overall diameter is 21 mm, and the maker gives a minimum bending radius of 6 times the diameter. The pump-house enclosure is outdoors and gets wet when the yard is washed down. The van has indoor-type glands with no outer seal, and outdoor-type glands with a seal and shroud.

c2.title: Fire alarm cable at a Runaway Bay hotel
c2.text: At a hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, electrician Ms Andrea Taylor and trainee Jermaine Pryce are terminating mineral-insulated cable for the fire alarm sounders. Jermaine strips one cable end at 10 a.m., then goes to lunch, leaving it unsealed in the humid air of the plant room. After lunch he seals it. On the insulation test the reading starts at 50 MΩ and slowly drops over the next few minutes. Plastic cable ties are being used to hold some of the alarm cables to a tray.

c3.title: TV and CCTV in Portmore apartments
c3.text: Trainee Kevon Ellis and his supervisor Mr Dean Ferguson are wiring TV outlets and four CCTV cameras in a block of apartments in Portmore, St Catherine. They use RG6 coax with compression F connectors for the TV outlets, and RG59 coax with BNC connectors for the cameras. The coax from the satellite dish on the roof enters the building through the wall of the top-floor corridor. Kevon is fixing the coax along the skirting with a staple gun.

c4.title: A computer lab at a Highgate school
c4.text: Trainees Tashoya Bailey and Ryan Watson are installing Cat 6 cable for a computer lab at a high school in Highgate, St Mary. Each cable runs from a patch panel in the server cabinet to a wall outlet; the longest fixed run is 84 m, and each end will have a 5 m patch lead. Everything, including their patch leads, is to be wired to T568B. The school's tester shows the wire map of each link.

c5.title: A control panel at a Bog Walk factory
c5.text: At a juice factory in Bog Walk, St Catherine, technician Mr Leroy Hamilton and trainee Shanique Allen are terminating a 12-core screened control cable between a field instrument box and a control panel. The cable has an overall foil screen with a drain wire. The termination schedule lists each core number and its terminal at both ends, and says the screen is earthed at the control panel. The panel's terminals take fine-stranded cores.

questions.q: Which gland should Brittany fit at the pump-house enclosure?
o: An indoor gland, wrapped in tape outside
An outdoor gland with seal and shroud
Either type, since both grip the armour
No gland: a rubber grommet is enough
questions.why: Outdoors and in wash-down areas the gland must seal on the outer sheath, or water runs down the armour into the enclosure. The outdoor type has the seal, and the shroud protects the gland from water and corrosion.

questions.q: Which parts must be slid onto the cable before Brittany strips anything?
o: The earth tag and the locknut
The cone and the clamping ring
The shroud, back nut and seal
The gland body and its sealing washer
questions.why: The shroud and the back nut with its seal go over the outer sheath, so they must be on the cable before the end is prepared. The earth tag and locknut go on the gland body at the enclosure, and the cone goes under the armour.

questions.q: What is the tightest bending radius allowed for this cable?
o: 21 mm
63 mm
252 mm
126 mm
questions.why: 6 × the overall diameter: 6 × 21 = 126 mm. A tighter bend can damage the armour, the bedding and the insulation of the cores.

questions.q: How does the armour connect to the earth bar in the panel?
o: Through the armour clamp, gland body and earth tag
Through the outer sheath and the shroud of the gland
Through the bedding layer touching the earth bar
Through the locknut alone, with no other part needed
questions.why: The cone and clamping ring grip the armour and connect it to the gland body; the earth tag on the gland's entry thread is connected to the earth bar by a conductor. The sheath, shroud and bedding are insulating.

questions.q: On the insulation test, core to core reads 2,000 MΩ, but one core to the armour reads 0.05 MΩ. What is the most likely cause?
o: The cable is longer than usual for a pump
The tester was set to 500 V DC for the test
The outdoor gland was fitted at the pump end
Insulation cut while the armour was removed
questions.why: A very low reading between one core and the armour, while the cores read well, points to damaged insulation or bedding near the armour, typically from a hacksaw cut taken too deep. The end must be cut back and remade.

questions.q: What was Jermaine's mistake?
o: Leaving the stripped end unsealed
Testing the insulation after sealing it
Using a brass pot on a copper sheath
Terminating MI cable for fire alarms
questions.why: Magnesium oxide powder takes in moisture from the air. An end left open for hours in humid air soaks it up, so the end must be sealed as soon as possible after stripping.

questions.q: What should Jermaine do about the falling reading?
o: Accept it, as 50 MΩ was the first reading
Wrap tape round the pot to keep out more damp
Cut back past the damp part, reseal and retest
Test again at a higher voltage until it is steady
questions.why: A falling reading means moisture in the cable or seal, and it will get worse. Cut the end back past the damp section, strip and seal again, and retest: the reading should be high and steady.

questions.q: Why should the plastic cable ties holding alarm cables to the tray be replaced?
o: They make the cables run too hot in the tray
They melt in a fire and let cables fall
They are not allowed with red-sheathed cable
They block the fire alarm signals
questions.why: Fire alarm cables must stay in place and working during a fire. Plastic ties melt, and fallen cables can be damaged or trap firefighters, so metal clips or fire-rated fixings are used.

questions.q: A TV gets no picture, and a meter shows the centre of the new F connector joined to its screen. What is the likely cause?
o: The compression tool squeezed the connector
The coax is 75 ohm instead of 50 ohm cable
The jacket was stripped with a coax stripper
A braid strand touching the centre
questions.why: Continuity between centre and screen is a short circuit, and the usual cause is a stray braid strand touching the centre conductor. Remake the end, folding the braid back neatly and trimming loose strands.

questions.q: Why should Kevon stop stapling the coax to the skirting?
o: Staples crush it and change its impedance
Staples make the coax carry mains voltage
Coax must never be fixed to any surface
Staples earth the screen at each fixing
questions.why: A staple that squashes coax changes the spacing between centre and screen, and so its impedance, causing signal loss and reflections. Use clips made for coax, fitted without crushing it.

questions.q: What does the code usually require where the dish's coax enters the building?
o: A BNC connector in place of the F-type
A 50 ohm cable for the inside length
Its screen earthed via an earthing block
A fuse in the centre conductor of the coax
questions.why: An outdoor coax can bring lightning surges into the building. Earthing (grounding) its screen through an earthing block at the entry point gives the surge a path to earth before it reaches the equipment.

questions.q: How far should the centre conductor stick out of a fitted F connector?
o: Flush with the face, or just inside it
About 20 mm, so it reaches deep inside
It should be folded back over the braid
As the maker gives, often about 2 mm
questions.why: The centre conductor forms the connector's pin, so it must stick out the short length the maker states, often about 2 mm. Too short makes a poor contact; too long can bend or short inside the outlet.

questions.q: Tashoya lays out the wires for one end of a patch lead. Which wire belongs in position 3?
o: White-orange
White-green
Blue
Orange
questions.why: The T568B order is white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown, so position 3 is white-green. In T568A, the orange and green pairs change places.

questions.q: At the patch panel, Ryan untwists about 40 mm of each pair to make punching down easier. What is the problem?
o: The cable becomes too short to reach the outlet
The punch-down tool cannot cut untwisted wire
It raises crosstalk and can make the link fail
Untwisted wire carries more current and heats
questions.why: The twists cancel interference and crosstalk. Untwisting more than about 13 mm weakens that, and the link can fail its test or run slowly. Keep the twists right up to the contacts.

questions.q: Is the longest link, with its two 5 m patch leads, within the limit?
o: Yes: the channel is 94 m, within the 100 m limit
No: any run over 80 m must be changed to fibre
No: the fixed cable must not be more than 50 m
Yes: twisted-pair data cable has no length limit
questions.why: 84 m of fixed cable plus 10 m of patch leads is 94 m. The limit is 90 m of fixed cable and 100 m for the whole channel, so this link is within both.

questions.q: The wire map shows pins 1 and 2 crossed with pins 3 and 6 at one end of a lead. What has gone wrong?
o: One wire in the orange pair is broken
One end was wired to T568A, not T568B
The blue and brown pairs are reversed
The cable is too long for the tester
questions.why: T568A and T568B differ only in swapping the orange and green pairs, which sit on pins 1, 2, 3 and 6. One end made to the wrong standard gives exactly this crossed-pair result. Remake that end.

questions.q: At the field instrument box, what should be done with the screen and drain wire?
o: Connect the drain wire to the box's earth stud
Twist the drain wire round one of the signal cores
Leave the foil and drain wire hanging loose inside
Cut them back and insulate them
questions.why: The schedule earths the screen at the panel only. Earthing it at both ends can create an earth loop. At the field end the screen and drain wire are cut back and insulated, so they cannot touch the enclosure or a terminal.

questions.q: Shanique tins the stranded core ends with solder before putting them into the screw terminals. Why does Mr Hamilton stop her?
o: Solder creeps under the screw and the joint loosens
Solder makes the cores too stiff to mark them
Tinned cores can no longer be tested for continuity
Solder blocks the signal in an instrument cable
questions.why: Under the steady pressure of a screw, solder slowly flows, the clamping force falls and the joint can work loose and overheat. Fine-stranded cores get crimped bootlace ferrules instead.

questions.q: When should Shanique fit the core markers?
o: After all the cores are connected, from memory
Only on the cores that are not colour-coded
Before cutting to length, from the schedule
Only at the control-panel end of the cable
questions.why: Marking each core from the schedule before it is cut and terminated means no core gets mixed up, and both ends can be traced later. Markers go on every core at both ends.

questions.q: A trainee wants to find out whether an optical fibre is carrying light. What should he use?
o: His eye, glancing quickly into the connector
An optical power meter, never his own eye
A multimeter set to its continuity range
A torch shone into the far end of the fibre
questions.why: Fibre systems use invisible infrared light that can damage the eye without you seeing anything. An optical power meter shows whether light is present. A multimeter cannot test glass.
